method_note: Read the whole target. Re-queried 45 repositories with read-only gh api (licence, archived flag, pushed_at, stars) and read README heads for the claims that carry disclaimers, moves, licences or mechanisms. Fetched the GS1 resolver standard page and test suite page, and the GitLab UNTP page. Checked engine mapping against docs/reference/capabilities.md. No live DPP system was called. Metadata sweep results are grouped into one claim with a shared evidence note.

The capabilities table lists no linkset check.

checked.evidence: The page is titled as the GS1 Digital Link Resolver Test Suite and tests against version 1.2.1 of the resolver standard. It is an interactive web tool; individual test cases are not listed on the page. The file does not record the standard version (1.2.1, August 2026), which is a useful missed item.

missed_items.fact: The current resolver standard is version 1.2.1, ratified in August 2026 (PDF dated 2026-08-07). It defines the linkset response by Accept media type. The target file names the standard but never pins a version, which an identifier.resolve oracle needs.

missed_items.topic: GS1 resolver test suite target version
missed_items.fact: The GS1 Digital Link Resolver Test Suite page states that it tests against version 1.2.1 of the resolver standard. It is an interactive web tool and would be a live call, so it must not be used in tests.

The Dataspace Protocol specification now lives at eclipse-dataspace-protocol-base/DataspaceProtocol, with a rendered site at eclipse-dataspace-protocol-base.github.io/DataspaceProtocol. The old IDS repository README names both.
aas-core3.0-python is now under the eclipse-aascw organisation; other aas-core-works repositories may have moved too and old URLs only redirect.
aas.validate is experimental in capabilities.md, so every 'aas.validate applies' mapping in the file should read 'experimental'.
The openepcis-dpp-ready README makes claims about which CEN/CLC JTC 24 standards were published; these are vendor statements (secondary_only) and must not enter the catalogue as facts.

overall: The file is reliable on repository metadata. Of 45 repositories re-queried through the GitHub API, licence, archived flag, star count and push time matched in every case except the aas-core entry, whose organisation changed to eclipse-aascw so the name and URL are stale. README-derived statements (disclaimers, project end date, moved specification, BSL-1.1, preview version, digest mechanism) all held up. Engine mappings match the capability table, but they omit that aas.validate is experimental. Weak spots are untested claims such as test directories (stated as 'not inspected' by the file) and the missing version of the GS1 resolver standard. No rule 5 problem was found: the file names EN numbers only as labels and does not describe their content. Stars and push times are snapshots and will drift.
